sections.authorBiography: Hermann Hesse was born on 2 July 1877 in Calw, in the German kingdom of Württemberg, into a family of Pietist Protestant missionaries with deep ties to India: his father, Johannes Hesse, had served with the Basel Mission there, his mother, Marie Gundert, was born in India, and his grandfather Hermann Gundert was a missionary scholar of Malayalam. As a teenager Hesse ran away from the Protestant seminary at Maulbronn and went through a severe personal crisis before training as a bookseller in Tübingen and Basel. His first success, Peter Camenzind (1904), let him live as a writer. During the First World War he published an appeal against nationalist hatred and was denounced in the German press; after the war, amid a breakdown of his marriage and his health, he moved to Montagnola in Switzerland and became a Swiss citizen in 1924. His major novels include Demian (1919), Siddhartha (1922), Steppenwolf (1927) and The Glass Bead Game (1943). He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946 and died in Montagnola on 9 August 1962.
sections.historicalContext: Siddhartha is set in India in the time of the Buddha (around the fifth century BCE), but it was written in Europe just after the First World War, when many young Germans had lost faith in the nation, the church and their parents' certainties. Hesse had grown up among books and stories about India, travelled in 1911 to Ceylon (Sri Lanka), Malaya and Sumatra, and read the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and Buddhist texts in translation. He was also influenced by psychoanalysis; he underwent analysis with a follower of Carl Jung around 1916–17. The novel is a European writer's imagined India: it uses Hindu and Buddhist ideas (Atman, Brahman, the Samanas, nirvana, Om, the cycle of Sansara) to tell a very personal story about finding one's own way.

publicationAndReception.then: In Germany in the 1920s the book was respected but not one of Hesse's bestsellers; readers knew him better for Demian. Some critics found its Indian setting exotic decoration for a European story of the self.
publicationAndReception.now: Siddhartha became a worldwide success after the 1951 English translation, especially in the 1960s, when the American counterculture embraced Hesse as a prophet of self-discovery and Eastern spirituality. It is now one of the most widely translated German novels and is taught in world literature and philosophy classes. Scholars today also discuss its limits: it is a Western, idealized picture of Indian religion, and its hero is not the Buddha but a seeker who rejects every teacher, including the Buddha.

sections.overview: Siddhartha, the gifted son of a Brahmin priest, leaves home with his friend Govinda to search for the truth about the self. He tries the life of the wandering ascetics, meets the Buddha, enters the world of a great city and a beautiful courtesan, and finally comes to a river and a ferryman. The book follows one man's whole life as he tests every path to wisdom.

spoilerOverview.text: Siddhartha rejects the Buddha's teaching (though he reveres him), learns love from Kamala and business from Kamaswami, grows rich and empty, nearly drowns himself, and is renewed by the river. He becomes Vasudeva's fellow ferryman, meets Kamala again as she dies, and loses his son, who runs away. Listening to the river he hears the unity of all voices in Om; in old age he tells Govinda that wisdom cannot be taught, and Govinda sees all things in his face.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Siddhartha.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Siddhartha: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Siddhartha and argue how its meaning changes over the novel and why that change matters to experience versus teaching.
Analyze a central character's choices in Siddhartha. Argue whether the novel judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.
Two readers disagree about whether Siddhartha finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of the unity of all things. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the chapter and paragraph (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.
